blk_part_01_part_1_one_name_many_kinds_o.text: “Curry” does not describe one fixed recipe. Across South Asia and India, different regions have developed many local dishes using their own ingredients and spice combinations. Later, Britain produced commercial curry powder: a prepared mixture that gave cooks a more regular result. This mixture eventually reached Japan, where cooks changed the sauce to suit rice and local meals.

blk_part_03_part_3_curry_arrives_and_dev.text: Commercial curry powder entered Japan in the early Meiji period. Japanese cooks thickened the sauce and served it with rice. Curry then became popular in homes, towns, and school lunches. One theory connects this development with the Japanese Navy. A British Royal Navy curry-flavored stew was adapted into a thick sauce that worked with rice and offered a practical meal containing meat and vegetables. Retired sailors later helped spread this naval style.

blk_part_05_part_5_why_chili_feels_hot.text: The heat of chili is not the same as the physical temperature of food. Chili peppers contain a compound called capsaicin. Capsaicin activates a receptor in the body called TRPV1. This receptor also responds to real heat, so the brain can receive a heat-like signal even when the food itself is not unusually hot.

blk_part_05_part_5_why_chili_feels_hot.text: That is why spicy curry can create a burning sensation in the mouth. The experience may continue after you swallow because the body is still responding to capsaicin. Its sources include varied South Asian food traditions and British commercial curry powder. Important changes in Japan included a thicker sauce, service with rice, practical meat-and-vegetable meals, and convenient products for home cooking. The result became familiar in homes and school lunches.
